lead: An aircraft rarely knows its position directly. It measures one number, such as the time a radio pulse takes to come back or the direction a signal arrives from, and that number puts it somewhere on a line on the map: a line of position. Two lines that cross give a fix. This chapter sets up the geometry every later aid uses: the Earth model, the words for direction, the shapes of the lines and how the crossing angle sets the error.
prereq: You need basic trigonometry (sine and cosine rules). Height above the ground comes from the air data instruments: see Air data instruments: airspeed indicator and altimeter.

blocks.text: Navigation starts with a model of the Earth. The simplest is a sphere. A meridian is a half great circle from pole to pole; the equator is the great circle midway between the poles. Latitude φ is the angle north or south of the equator, 0° to 90°. Longitude λ is the angle east or west of the Greenwich meridian, 0° to 180°.

The real Earth is flattened at the poles, so satellite navigation uses the WGS-84 datum: an Earth-centred coordinate system plus a reference ellipsoid (semi-major axis a = 6 378 137 m, flattening f = 1/298.257223563). Satellite positions are points in space in that frame; only ground positions (latitude, longitude, height) are measured on the ellipsoid.

A great circle is the shortest path on the surface between two points; its plane passes through the Earth's centre. A rhumb line cuts every meridian at the same angle, so it can be flown on one constant track. It is longer than the great circle except along a meridian or the equator.
The nautical mile (nm) is 1852 m, first defined as one minute of arc of latitude. One knot (kt) is one nautical mile per hour. Aviation measures distance in nautical miles and speed in knots.
cos Δσ = sin φ₁ sin φ₂ + cos φ₁ cos φ₂ cos Δλ,    d = R · Δσ
blocks.where: Δσ is the angle between the two points seen from the Earth's centre, in radians; φ₁ and φ₂ are the two latitudes; Δλ is the difference of longitude; R ≈ 6371 km is the mean Earth radius; d is the great-circle distance in the units of R.

blocks.text: Heading is where the nose points, measured clockwise from north. Always say whether it is true or magnetic.

Track is the direction the aircraft actually moves over the ground. Wind makes track differ from heading. Drift is the angle from heading to track, counted positive to the right: track = heading + drift. True airspeed is measured along the heading; ground speed along the track.

Bearing is the direction of one point from another, so always name both points. Over short distances the bearing of the station from the aircraft and of the aircraft from the station differ by 180°; on long great-circle legs the convergence of the meridians adds to that.

A radial is a line leaving a station, named by its magnetic bearing from that station. An aircraft on the 030 radial is somewhere on the line that leaves the station towards 030°. Its heading can be anything.
A line of position (LOP) is the set of all points where one measurement would give the same reading. The true position lies on it. Three shapes matter in this unit.

items: Circle. A range from a known station fixes distance but not direction, so the LOP is a circle centred on the station. DME and radar give circles; satellite ranges give spheres.
Straight line. A bearing from a known station fixes direction but not distance, so the LOP is a line leaving the station. VOR, ADF and the ILS localizer give such lines.
Hyperbola. The difference of the ranges to two stations is constant along a hyperbola that has the two stations as its foci.

blocks.text: Fix methods are named after what they measure: rho-theta (a range ρ and a bearing θ from one station), rho-rho (two ranges) and theta-theta (two bearings). Three lines almost never meet at one point; they form a small triangle called the cocked hat, and the fix is taken inside it.

The cut angle θ is the angle at which two LOPs cross. Each line has an error σ measured across the line (along the line the measurement says nothing). When the lines cross at a shallow angle, a small sideways shift of either line slides the crossing point a long way.

blocks.where: σ is the 1-sigma error of each line of position, measured at right angles to the line; θ is the cut angle. At θ = 90° the fix error equals σ; at θ = 30° it doubles.

sections.h3: Reference frames, and accuracy against repeatability

blocks.text: ECEF (Earth-centred, Earth-fixed): origin at the Earth's centre, x-axis through the equator at Greenwich, z-axis through the North Pole. It turns with the Earth, so a ground point keeps fixed coordinates; satellite orbits are broadcast in it.

Local NED (north, east, down) has its origin at the aircraft; heading and track live here. The inertial frame does not turn with the Earth, which turns at 15.04° per hour relative to it; gyros and accelerometers sense motion relative to this frame.

Accuracy is how close a reported position is to the true one. Repeatability is how close repeated reports are to each other. A system can be repeatable and wrong: a fixed bias moves every fix by the same 200 m. Calibration removes bias and averaging removes noise; neither does the other's job.

examples.question: Two DME stations A and B are 130 nm apart. The aircraft reads 50 nm to A and 120 nm to B. (a) Find the cut angle at which the two range circles cross. (b) Find the aircraft's distance from A measured along AB, and its distance from the line AB. (c) Judge the fix.
steps: The two range circles cross at the aircraft. The angle between two circles at a crossing equals the angle between their radii there, so the cut angle is the angle at the aircraft in triangle A–aircraft–B, whose sides are 50, 120 and 130 nm.
Check: 50² + 120² = 16 900 = 130², so the triangle is right-angled at the aircraft.
Two circles cross twice, once on each side of AB; the route or a VOR radial says which crossing is the aircraft.
sin 90° = 1, so the fix error equals the error of one line: the best a two-range fix can give.
examples.answer: θ = 90°; the aircraft is 19.23 nm from A along AB and 46.15 nm off the line, on the side the route puts it. The fix is as good as a two-range fix gets.

examples.question: Find the great-circle distance from Chennai (13.0° N, 80.2° E) to Delhi (28.6° N, 77.1° E) in kilometres and nautical miles, and the time at a ground speed of 450 kt.
steps: Check: one degree of great circle is 60 nm, and 15.86 × 60 = 952 nm, the same answer.
examples.answer: About 1764 km or 953 nm; at 450 kt it takes about 127 minutes (2 h 7 min).

traps: Heading, track and bearing are three different things. A radial of 030 says where the aircraft is relative to the station; the nose may point anywhere.
Outbound on the 030 radial you track 030°; inbound on the same radial you track 210°. Forgetting the 180° flip costs marks.
In σ ÷ sin θ, σ is the error across each line, not along it. Along the line the measurement gives no information at all.
A small cocked hat does not prove a good fix. If all three lines share one bias, such as a common timing error, they make a tiny triangle around a wrong point.

quiz.a: The set of all points at which one particular measurement would give the same reading; the true position lies somewhere on it.

quiz.q: Give the nautical mile in metres and define the knot.
quiz.a: 1 nm = 1852 m; 1 knot = 1 nautical mile per hour.

quiz.q: An aircraft is on the 090 radial of a VOR. What does that tell you, and what does it not tell you?
quiz.a: It lies on the line leaving the station towards 090° magnetic, so it is east of the station. It gives no distance, no heading and no track.

quiz.q: Two DME ranges read 50 nm and 70 nm from stations 100 nm apart. Find the cut angle and the fix error if each line has a 1-sigma error of 1 nm.
Two LOPs cross at 30° with a 1-sigma error of 1 nm each. Compare this fix with a 90° cut, and say why a small cocked hat can still be wrong.
quiz.a: Fix error = 1 ÷ sin 30° = 2 nm, twice the 1 nm of a 90° cut; the error ellipse stretches along the bisector of the narrow angle. A small cocked hat shows only that the random errors are small; a bias common to all lines (a clock error, a wrongly surveyed station) moves all of them together and leaves a small triangle around a wrong point.

beyond: Not for the exam. The σ ÷ sin θ idea returns in satellite navigation as dilution of precision, written for four satellites as a matrix. Required navigation performance (RNP) sets how large this error may be on each route, and the aircraft monitors it. Search next for WGS-84 parameters, great-circle sailing and required navigation performance.

figure.caption: The worked example: the 50 nm circle round A and the 120 nm circle round B cross at right angles, 19.23 nm along AB and 46.15 nm off it. The panel shows why the cut angle matters: the same ±σ bands give a box twice as long at 30°.
